title: Impact of sustained professional development in STEM on outcome measures in a diverse urban district
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether sustained professional development (PD) in STEM, centered on project-based learning (PBL) and professional learning communities, improved classroom practice and student outcomes in a diverse urban school district. The study was motivated by concerns about weak K-12 STEM achievement, particularly in mathematics and science, and the need for reform-oriented teacher support that could translate into better classroom instruction and student performance.

The intervention was a three-year, district-level PD program delivered by a university-based team to teachers in three urban high schools. Teachers received 180 total hours of PD focused on STEM PBL structure, facilitation, assessment, classroom learning environments, and collaborative professional learning communities. Classroom observations were used to assess fidelity of PBL implementation, and student outcomes were measured using state accountability test scores in mathematics, science, and reading. The study also included focus group interviews with teachers to capture their perceptions of the PD and PBL implementation.

The findings showed that higher-fidelity implementation was associated with larger gains in student achievement, especially in the school with the strongest implementation, where mathematics and science scores increased substantially. Schools with weaker implementation showed smaller gains or negative effects. Teachers reported that PBL increased student engagement and participation, but also noted challenges related to time, materials, and accountability pressures. Overall, the paper concludes that sustained, systemic PD can support STEM instructional reform when implementation is strong and supported by school-level collaboration.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a longitudinal quasi-experimental mixed-methods study with propensity score matching and observational fidelity data, but it is not randomized and has important attrition and implementation-variability concerns. The qualitative components strengthen interpretation, yet overall credibility is below a well-designed RCT/QED standard.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports large positive effects in the highest-fidelity school, especially for science (d=2.03) and mathematics (d=1.41), which exceeds the threshold for a large impact. However, effects are mixed across schools and groups, so the strongest impact is conditional on implementation fidelity rather than uniform across settings.

interventions.use_case: Sustained STEM professional development supporting project-based learning (PBL) implementation in urban high school mathematics and science classrooms, including teacher PLCs and classroom observations to improve enactment fidelity.

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics outcomes varied substantially by school and by implementation fidelity. In HS3, student mathematics scores improved strongly with the longitudinal group showing d=1.41 and the matched group d=0.62; HS2 showed moderate gains in the longitudinal group (d=0.66) but negative change in the matched group (d=-0.23); HS1 showed a small positive matched-group effect (d=0.34) but a negative longitudinal effect (d=-0.16).
finding.measure: State accountability mathematics test scores (TAKS raw scores)
finding.study_size: n=60 per school sample frame; longitudinal groups retained 53-56 students and matched groups retained 19-57 students depending on school
finding.std_deviation: pooled SD reported in Table 2, exact value not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Science outcomes also depended on implementation fidelity. HS3 showed very large gains for both the longitudinal and matched groups (d=2.03 and d=0.92), HS2 showed a small positive longitudinal effect (d=0.73) and essentially no effect in the matched group (d=0.04), and HS1 showed a small positive longitudinal effect (d=0.22) but a negative matched-group effect (d=-0.08).
finding.measure: State accountability science test scores (TAKS raw scores)
finding.study_size: n=60 per school sample frame; longitudinal groups retained 53-56 students and matched groups retained 19-57 students depending on school
finding.std_deviation: pooled SD reported in Table 2, exact value not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Reading was not an intended target of the intervention, but the study reported spillover-like changes that were inconsistent across schools and groups. Effects ranged from negative to positive, including HS1 longitudinal d=0.26 and matched d=-0.48, HS2 longitudinal d=-0.34 and matched d=-0.35, and HS3 longitudinal d=0.36 and matched d=-0.80, suggesting no reliable literacy benefit.
finding.measure: State accountability reading test scores (TAKS raw scores)
finding.study_size: n=60 per school sample frame; longitudinal groups retained 53-56 students and matched groups retained 19-57 students depending on school
finding.std_deviation: pooled SD reported in Table 2, exact value not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Teachers consistently reported that PBL increased student engagement, including engagement among typically unengaged students. This qualitative finding appeared across five of six focus groups and was described as one of the strongest benefits of the sustained PD/PBL model, but no quantitative engagement scale was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher focus group reports of student engagement and participation

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative data suggested that PBL increased students' participation in collaborative small-group roles and supported more active involvement in lab/project work. Teachers described broader participation and more students taking on roles in the project process, but these outcomes were not quantified with a standardized measure.
finding.measure: Teacher focus group reports of collaboration and role participation during PBL
